headline: CIA - Black Tie Optional - Review : Down To Party
snippet: I think this episode of CIA has been my favourite of the whole show so far. I loved every single aspect of it but most of all, I loved being able to see Bill and Colin really lean on each other and know that they can trust each other when put in serious situations. Episode one Colin and Bill would not have been able to cohesively deal with the undercover op going wrong and it’s so fun to see where they are now. One of the best things they have done that has bled from the first season is having an overarching storyline. I enjoyed the mole storyline last year but I’m definitely more interested in what happened with Bill’s dad and Felix Vincent. It ties everything together so well. The past couple episodes, Colin has seemed very in touch with his emotions and it’s been so great to watch. Even if he does use jokes to get through his feelings, it’s wonderful to see a stoic man’s emotions portrayed on screen. Bill is also really going through it this season, I did like him questioning if he should really be looking into his dad’s past or not. I do think there is a level of grief that he is looking into his dad because he’s no longer alive. The set up for Bill’s father’s watch was so good, normally I see it coming but when Colin found the chip it made all the more sense why it was mentioned that Bill had it at the start of the episode. The suspense of what Bill’s dad was doing and why Felix went rogue makes sure that I am tuning in each episode. I can’t wait to see what they uncover next!

headline: From golden population to golden workforce: The human side of Vietnam's AI vision
snippet: Dr Tan Hong Ming, Assistant Dean (Digital Operations), NUS Business School (sixth from left), with Ms Tara Bal, Head of Corporate Communications, NUS Business School (fifth from right), together with representatives from the Vietnamese media. HANOI, VIETNAM - Media OutReach Newswire - 27 October 2026 - As Vietnam pursues its ambition of becoming a high-income developed economy by 2045, artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to play a growing role in supporting productivity and innovation. Alongside technology adoption, developing the skills and management capabilities to apply AI effectively is becoming an important part of the country's workforce agenda. A 2026 study commissioned by Amazon Web Services (AWS) found that 26 per cent of Vietnamese businesses have adopted AI, up from 18 per cent a year earlier. However, 61 per cent of adopters remain at the experimentation stage, while 87 per cent of surveyed employers consider reskilling existing employees important to their AI strategies. Vietnam has also prioritised workforce development through its national AI human resources development programme, approved in August 2026. The programme includes plans to equip around 10 million workers with basic AI skills by 2030, alongside developing specialised AI talent and strengthening AI education. Dr Tan Hong Ming, Assistant Dean (Digital Operations) at the National University of Singapore (NUS) Business School, said workforce development needs to extend beyond technical proficiency. "AI literacy is only the starting point. The bigger challenge is whether organisations know how to redesign work around AI. A company can train every employee to use AI tools and still see little improvement in productivity if its processes and management practices remain unchanged. This is why leadership capability matters just as much as technical skills," said Dr Tan at a media engagement session in Hanoi. From adopting AI to creating business value As AI tools become more accessible, businesses face decisions about where the technology can be applied, how existing work processes may need to change and what employees need to learn. Dr Tan believes that while AI can improve productivity by automating tasks, organisations must also consider how its growing use affects the way employees learn and develop expertise. "Struggle is an important part of learning. We develop expertise and judgement by working through difficult problems, making mistakes and figuring things out for ourselves. AI can now take away much of that struggle by providing answers almost instantly. While this improves productivity, we need to be careful that we are not also removing the experiences that help people learn and grow. Organisations need to rethink how employees develop these capabilities in an AI-enabled workplace," he said. Beyond developing AI literacy, organisations need to consider how employees assess AI-generated information, how managers incorporate the technology into workflows and how senior leaders oversee its use in business decisions. Rethinking how professionals learn The growing use of AI also raises questions about how professionals acquire the experience and judgement needed to take on more complex responsibilities. While AI can help generate information and recommendations, learning to make business decisions still requires opportunities to question assumptions, evaluate competing perspectives and work through problems without complete information. NUS Business School is piloting an AI-enabled business simulation that allows MBA and Executive MBA students to practise these capabilities. The simulation uses ScholAIstic, a generative AI platform developed by the NUS AI Centre for Educational Technologies (AICET). Dr Emir Hrnjić, Senior Lecturer in Finance at NUS Business School, has been working with AICET to adapt and refine the platform's capabilities for management education, creating AI-simulated executives whom students interview before making business recommendations. Professor Teo Chung Piaw, Dean of NUS Business School, said the growing capabilities of AI require business schools to examine not only what students learn, but also how they develop and apply their knowledge. "The role of business education is changing as AI becomes part of how organisations operate and make decisions. We cannot simply introduce new technology into existing teaching methods and assume that learning will improve. Business schools need to examine what students should learn, how they acquire that knowledge and how their ability to apply it is assessed. Our approach is to use AI to create more opportunities for students to think critically, engage with different perspectives and exercise independent judgement," said Prof Teo. Beyond preparing graduates for the workplace, postgraduate programmes and Executive Education can provide opportunities for working professionals and senior executives to update their knowledge and develop the capabilities needed to manage technological and organisational change. Building Vietnam's golden workforce Vietnam's Vision 2045 places continued emphasis on productivity, innovation and the development of higher-value industries. As AI becomes more widely adopted, higher education and professional training can contribute by equipping graduates, managers and senior executives with the capabilities to apply technology effectively in business. Dr Tan said the country's demographic advantage provides a foundation for developing these capabilities throughout people's careers. "Vietnam's demographic advantage gives it an important opportunity, but a young workforce alone does not guarantee economic success. The real opportunity is to develop a workforce that can continuously learn, adapt and create value alongside AI. If Vietnam can combine its human capital with the effective adoption of AI, it can turn its golden population into a golden workforce," he said. The school has consistently ranked first in Asia by independent publications and agencies, such as The Financial Times and Quacquarelli Symonds, in recognition of the quality of its programmes, faculty research and graduates. headline: Falmouth deputy mayor hails Wakefield’s rising athletic stars
snippet: FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Wakefield’s rising track and field stars are proof that greatness can emerge from rural Jamaica, says councillor for the division Jonathan Bartley, who has lauded Jabari Matheson, Sanjay Seymour, and Daniella Dixon for bringing pride to Trelawny through their athletic achievements. The trio were honoured during the National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony in Water Square, Falmouth, for their outstanding performances and contributions to sport. Bartley said the recognition was an important way of encouraging young people to pursue excellence, particularly at a time when some were becoming discouraged by their circumstances or failing to realise their potential. “They are from a little rural community where they could just sit back and give up. But they pushed forward and showed that good things can come out of the countryside,” said Bartley, who is also deputy mayor of Falmouth. He added that the athletes had demonstrated that young people could excel both academically and on the field, providing positive examples for others in Wakefield and across the parish. Bartley also praised the trio for the pride they had brought to Trelawny, noting that their achievements reflected well on the community and the wider parish. “I really like how all of them big up Trelawny and how they make Trelawny look good. They are from Wakefield; they are from the parish,” he said. He encouraged the young athletes to draw inspiration from Jamaica’s sprinting greats Usain Bolt and Veronica Campbell-Brown as they continue to develop their careers and pursue further success on the international stage. The three were recognised by the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC) for their achievements at the national and international levels, as well as their leadership and positive influence on young people. Matheson, a student of William Knibb Memorial High School and former student of Wakefield Primary School, has distinguished himself in the 200-metre and 400-metre events. He captained William Knibb’s track and field team to victory in the 4x400-metre relay at Western Championships, where the team broke the existing record. The team also secured a top-10 finish in the 4x100-metre relay at the national championships. Matheson further demonstrated his potential in Canada, where he broke the Under-20 200-metre record and earned medals in both sprint events. Seymour, a former William Knibb student, enjoyed an impressive 2026 season, winning the Under-20 200-metre gold medal at the Carifta Games in Grenada before successfully defending his Class One 100-metre and 200-metre titles at the ISSA/GraceKennedy Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships. He also won the Class One 100-metre event at Western Championships. His international campaign culminated in a bronze medal as a member of Jamaica’s men’s 4x100-metre relay team at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships. Seymour has also excelled academically, earning six Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate subjects. He received the award for the sportsperson with the best academic results at graduation, along with the prestigious William Knibb Ambassador Award. Dixon, meanwhile, has established herself as another promising talent from Wakefield. A Western Championships record holder, she has represented Jamaica at the Under-17 and Under-20 levels in the 400 metres and 4x400-metre relay. In July 2026, she finished third in the 400 metres while representing Jamaica in Mexico. She later clocked a personal-best 52.64 seconds at the Jamaica Under-20 trials in Kingston before advancing to the semi-finals of the 400 metres at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships, where she finished fifth in her semi-final. Now a scholarship recipient at Holmwood Technical High School, Dixon continues to balance her academic and athletic pursuits while contributing to community sporting activities and encouraging her peers. Wakefield has also produced other notable track and field talents, including Shanoya Douglas, further underscoring the community’s contribution to Jamaica’s rich athletics tradition. She was also awarded by the TMC in a recent civic ceremony. The recognition of Matheson, Seymour and Dixon highlights Wakefield’s contribution to Jamaica’s track and field talent pool and the promise of a new generation aspiring to represent the country with distinction. The National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony was hosted by the Trelawny Municipal Corporation in partnership with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, recognising individuals whose achievements and contributions continue to bring distinction to the parish and the country.

headline: Japan To Allow Sale Of Emergency Contraception Pills Without Prescription - BW Healthcare World
snippet: In a big step towards joining dozens of other nations that currently allow such sales at pharmacies, Japan's health ministry announced Monday that it will allow the trial sale of emergency contraceptives without a prescription beginning this summer, Kyodo News reported. A ministry panel has approved the sale of so called morning after pills at pharmacies that have trained pharmacists, private rooms, and are available on weekends, nights and holidays through March. They must also be able to coordinate with obstetrics and gynaecology clinics in the area. As per the current rules, women, even sexual assault victims, have to travel to a clinic or hospital for a prescription to purchase emergency contraception, which works best within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, as per Kyodo News. Kyodo News is a Japan-based news agency established in November 1945. A ministry panel debated selling the medicine without a prescription in 2017, but the ministry stopped short of giving the green light, with critics claiming that making a morning-after pill available would encourage irresponsible use of the drug after intercourse. According to research conducted by the Health, Labour, and Welfare Ministry, emergency contraception has been available without a prescription in around 90 countries, according to Kyodo News. Clinical research done both at home and abroad show that emergency contraceptive tablets have an 80 per cent efficacy rate. Medical professionals have urged for increased access to the medicine in Japan, arguing that it might give rape victims a vital recourse while potentially lowering the need for abortions. Following the Cabinet's approval of various gender equality policies in late 2020, debates related to the over-the-counter distribution of emergency contraception pills have resumed. From the end of December to the beginning of January, the health ministry received 46,312 public comments, with the vast majority in favour of the trial sale, Kyodo News reported. (ANI)

headline: Trump Administration Invokes Defense Production Act for $150M Fuel Production
snippet: The Trump administration announced Thursday that it will invoke the Defense Production Act to allocate $150 million toward increasing U. S. production of gasoline and diesel. The Department of Energy stated in a press release that this funding is intended to boost refining output by millions of gallons per day, aiming to lower fuel costs for Americans who have been paying an average of more than $4 per gallon over the past three months. However, energy experts and industry representatives indicated that this measure is unlikely to provide short-term relief for household budgets. Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News that the initiative is "not going to have any impact" because global market forces, rather than domestic supply shortages, are driving current price levels. He noted that disruptions from the Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war have pushed crude oil prices to their highest levels since May, with Brent crude reaching $116 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate trading around $103 a barrel as of Friday. Domestic Production Exceeds Consumption The core issue identified by industry analysts is that the United States already produces more fuel than it consumes domestically. Data cited by experts shows that the U. S. produces approximately 9.5 million barrels of gasoline per day, while domestic consumption sits at 8.9 million barrels. Similarly, production of distillate fuel oil, which includes diesel, stands at around 5.3 million barrels per day against a consumption rate of 3.6 million barrels. Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, explained that because the U. S. exports about 1.4 million barrels of diesel daily, there is "no slack in U. S. refining." Consequently, political directives cannot immediately expand physical production capacity beyond current operational limits.

headline: UAE sets four levels for calculating private sector end-of-service gratuity
snippet: Abu Dhabi: The UAE Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation has set out four levels for calculating end-of-service gratuity for foreign workers in the private sector: fractions of a year, the first period, years of service and the maximum gratuity. The ministry said the gratuity is calculated at 21 days’ wages for each of the first five years of service and 30 days’ wages for each additional year. Workers are also entitled to gratuity for fractions of a year in proportion to the period worked, provided they have completed one continuous year of service. The total end-of-service gratuity must not exceed two years’ wages, in accordance with applicable regulations. The ministry explained through its social media accounts that employers are required to pay end-of-service benefits and any wages due to workers within 14 days of the termination of their contracts. It also highlighted an optional alternative system for end-of-service benefits, known as the savings system, which allows end-of-service benefits to be invested and grow through licensed and approved investment funds. The ministry also highlighted three channels for registering labour complaints related to domestic workers when disputes between workers and employers cannot be settled amicably. Complaints can be filed through the MOHRE UAE app, the ministry’s website or by contacting the Labour Claims and Consultation Centre on 80084. The ministry also outlined the benefits of the optional savings system, under which amounts allocated for the end-of-service gratuity of employees working in private sector companies are invested in leading investment funds approved by the Securities and Commodities Authority, allowing employees’ savings to grow through investment returns. It said the savings system aims to support the UAE’s economic system, enhance the protection and well-being of the country’s workforce, increase individual investment returns for beneficiaries and allow workers to make additional optional contributions. The system also aims to enhance the attractiveness and flexibility of the labour market by improving services provided to workers, while taking advantage of opportunities to invest funds in investment instruments for economic activities in the country.

headline: PNP to work with foreign counterparts in Thomas Markle probe
snippet: THE Philippine National Police (PNP) will work with law enforcement agencies abroad in looking into allegations linking the father of Meghan Markle, the duchess of Sussex, to the possession of child abuse and exploitation images. Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., PNP chief, emphasized the need for cross-border cooperation in investigating Thomas Markle, particularly the cases that may involve digital evidence and individuals with links to different countries. “The safety of our children remains a priority. Those who try to engage in child exploitation often extend beyond borders, and as such, it emphasizes the importance of strong coordination with our foreign counterparts,” Nartatez said. Authorities said the elder Markle possessed images of child abuse reportedly found among his belongings at his former home in Cebu. He reportedly has denied the allegations. Digital forensics on a laptop in the Markle house is being conducted and full results are expected to be released next week, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said. Nartatez said the PNP maintains a zero-tolerance policy against child exploitation and is committed to protecting minors from abuse, including forms of exploitation facilitated by digital platforms and cross-border networks. Markle, whose daughter is married to Britain's Prince Harry, had been living in Cebu until reportedly returning to the United States earlier this year. The British tabloid the Sun first reported last week that Markle's son, Thomas Markle Jr., had discovered the child abuse images while going through boxes found in his father's former home. On Friday, Meghan Markle said she was "deeply distressed" by accusations her father had possessed images of child abuse, adding she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous "troubling and disturbing" allegations. After the reports, Meghan said that in 2018 she had seen a letter sent to London's Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection making similar accusations. "It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said in a statement. London's Metropolitan police said it had passed on the information to the royal couple but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies. Meghan Markle and Prince Harry left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud. They made an unexpected return with their children to live in the United Kingdom in August.
